text: Picture the Nuremberg rallies. Hundreds of thousands of raised arms, one word thundering across the stadium.
And Hermann Goering, Reich Marshal, second most powerful man in Germany, cuts in.
General Franz Halder was sitting close enough to hear it. Goering said it out loud: the only one who really knows about the Reichstag is I, because I set it on fire.
Nine years earlier, that fire had handed Adolf Hitler the legal machinery for a dictatorship that was never once repealed.
By late February 1933, Hitler had been Chancellor for exactly four weeks, and he still did not have what he needed.
He led a coalition cabinet with only three Nazi ministers out of eleven.
An election was set for March 5th, and Hitler needed a real majority, not a borrowed one.
His own party's raid on Communist headquarters weeks earlier had turned up nothing but old pamphlets in a cellar.
Here is a detail most retellings skip: Hermann Goering was President of the Reichstag.
His official residence was connected to the Reichstag building itself by an underground passage, built to carry the central heating.
Shirer is blunt: it was where a plan was connived to burn the Reichstag down. The tunnel was the delivery route.
On the evening of February 27th, two dinners were underway a few streets apart in Berlin.
At the exclusive Herrenklub, Vice-Chancellor Franz von Papen was entertaining President Paul von Hindenburg.
Across town at Joseph Goebbels' home, Hitler had come to dine with friends, relaxed. Then the phone rang.
Goebbels wrote it down himself, that same night, in his diary.
A call came in from Ernst Hanfstaengl: the Reichstag is on fire. Goebbels declined even to mention it to the Fuehrer.
A few minutes later he believed it. Then he and Hitler were in a car racing at sixty miles an hour toward the scene of the crime.
Papen was closer. From the Herrenklub, he and Hindenburg saw it directly: a red glow through the windows.
The dome of the Reichstag looking as though it were illuminated by searchlights, a burst of flame and a swirl of smoke.
Papen bundled the elderly President into his car and drove straight for the fire.
Goering was already there when Hitler and Goebbels arrived, quite beside himself with excitement.
This is the beginning of the Communist revolution, he declared. Every Communist official must be shot where he is found.
That order came before a single fact about the fire had been established.
Inside the burning building, police found one man: Marinus van der Lubbe, a young Dutch council-communist.
A half-witted, feeble-minded pyromaniac, in Shirer's phrase, though he had a real communist background and had tried arson before.
Days earlier the SA had picked him up after he boasted he meant to try the Reichstag next. To the Nazis he was a godsend.
But the physical evidence, established later at trial in Leipzig, did not fit a lone arsonist.
Two and a half minutes after he entered, the great central hall was already fiercely burning, with nothing but his own shirt for tinder.
Trial experts testified the main fires had been set with substantial chemicals and gasoline, more than one man could carry.
That was Karl Ernst's job, a former hotel bellhop turned Berlin SA leader.
Through Goering's underground tunnel, Ernst led a detachment of storm troopers who scattered gasoline and self-igniting chemicals.
Van der Lubbe, wandering the same darkened building with his own small fires, had no idea he was not alone.
This is not speculation. It came out under oath, years later, at Nuremberg.
Hans Gisevius testified plainly: it was Goebbels who first thought of setting the Reichstag on fire.
Rudolf Diels swore that Goering knew exactly how the fire was to be started.
And Goering's own birthday boast was recalled at Nuremberg by General Franz Halder, who heard it firsthand.
Shirer's verdict: there is enough evidence to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that it was the Nazis who planned the arson.
alts: Rise and Fall of the Third Reich book

text: The morning after, February 28th, Hitler brought President Hindenburg a decree for the Protection of the People and the State.
It suspended seven sections of the constitution outright: freedom of expression, the press, assembly, privacy of mail, protection from searches.
This decree was never repealed. It remained the legal foundation of the Third Reich for the entirety of its twelve years.
The arrests began within hours. Roughly four thousand Communist officials were rounded up, including sitting Reichstag deputies.
Storm troopers in trucks broke into homes, dragging people to SA barracks to be beaten and tortured.
Communist and Social Democrat papers were shut down. Only the Nazis and their Nationalist allies were left free to campaign.
The Prussian government backed the story with an official statement claiming proof of a Communist plot.
On March 3rd, in Frankfurt, Goering told a crowd: my mission is only to destroy and exterminate, nothing more.
Even after all of it, Germans still did not hand Hitler a majority. On March 5th, the Nazis took 44 percent of the vote.
Hitler needed his Nationalist partners' seats just to scrape a majority, nowhere near the two-thirds for the Enabling Act.
Four Communists were headed to trial: Ernst Torgler, the party's parliamentary leader, who turned himself in.
And three Bulgarian Communists: Georgi Dimitroff, Blagoi Popov, and Vasil Tanev.
Dimitroff, acting as his own lawyer, turned the Leipzig trial into a public humiliation for Goering.
Goering snapped: out with you, you scoundrel. Dimitroff got the last word: are you afraid of my questions?
The verdict, in December 1933, was its own kind of scandal: Torgler and all three Bulgarians were acquitted outright.
Only van der Lubbe, who had confessed, was convicted and executed by guillotine.
That acquittal enraged Hitler and Goering. Within a month the right to try treason was stripped from the Supreme Court.
It was handed to a brand-new tribunal, the Volksgerichtshof, the People's Court. There was no appeal. It became the most feared court in the Reich.
Karl Ernst did not get to enjoy the outcome. In the Night of the Long Knives, June 1934, Ernst was murdered.
Killed along with three other SA men believed to have been his accomplices in setting the Reichstag on fire. They knew too much.
Six years later, in November 1939, a bomb went off in a Munich beer hall minutes after Hitler left.
Shirer, in Berlin at the time, wrote in his diary: most of us think it smells of another Reichstag fire.
The decree Hindenburg signed the morning after never was repealed. One fire. One signature. Twelve years.
